name: Lip implants (Permalip, Gore-Tex)

lead: Lip implants are solid strips or tubes placed in the lips for permanent added volume. People choose them for a fuller, more defined lip that does not need repeat treatments like filler.

The two materials most discussed are ePTFE (sold as Gore-Tex and similar products) and solid silicone (Permalip). The implant sits in or near the lip muscle and adds bulk, and ePTFE is porous so tissue grows into it. Reports date from the early 1990s, including a 2002 paper on a redesigned implant and a 2017 retrospective study of 100 women. Use has declined relative to fillers.

paras: A surgeon places the implant through a small incision, and the lips settle over the following weeks. People who want durable volume consider it alongside fillers and fat grafting. The implant stays in place unless it is removed.

Reported complications include infection, extrusion, migration, shrinkage and hardening in some patients. Removal may be required. Because it is permanent, changing the look later means another operation.

angle.text: Gore-Tex or silicone implants are chosen by people who want permanent lip volume, with a fuller, more defined lip visible after healing. They are discussed alongside fillers and fat grafting as the durable option. Published studies are mostly case series.

lead: Lip implants are solid, permanent inserts placed in the lips to increase volume, projection or definition. They are used by people who want fuller lips that do not need repeat injections: a strip or tube of material is placed through a small incision, usually at the mouth corner, and stays in the lip tissue. Two materials are most discussed: expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE, sold as Gore-Tex and under names such as Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm) and solid silicone (Permalip) [1][2].

Lip implants sit at the permanent end of a spectrum that runs from temporary products such as lip plumpers and hyaluronic acid fillers, through fat transfer, to surgical inserts. Practitioners who choose implants generally do so for a lasting result, and the implant can be removed or exchanged if the person is unhappy with it. A 2017 retrospective study of 100 women described the solid prosthesis as an innovation in aesthetic medicine and an emerging option for permanent results [3].

Published research consists mainly of case series and surgeon-authored technique papers rather than randomized trials. Reported complications include infection, extrusion, migration, shrinkage and hardening [4]. Use has declined relative to fillers; a 2006 survey article asked who was still using lip implants [5].
infobox: ePTFE (Gore-Tex; Advanta, UltraSoft, SoftForm); solid silicone (Permalip)
Strips and tubes of about 1.6 mm and 4.8 mm diameter [2]
3-4 days of noticeable swelling reported in one ePTFE series [4]

paras: ePTFE has a porous structure that tissue can grow into, and has been supplied to surgeons as strips and tubes of roughly 1.6 mm and 4.8 mm diameter [2][6]. The commercial names listed on Wikipedia for medical ePTFE used in the lips are Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm [2]. The material is placed in a channel created in the lip tissue, with the aim of a natural-feeling result that conforms to the lip's shape [7].

Grokipedia describes Permalip as a soft solid silicone elastomer, 3-5 mm thick and 55-65 mm long, inserted through small incisions at the mouth corners [6]. This description comes from an AI-generated encyclopedia and has not been independently verified. Implants of this type have also been used outside cosmetic practice: a 2020 cleft lip study included six PermaLip implants among surgical options to restore upper lip projection [8].

Wikipedia's overview of lip augmentation traces a sequence of materials: paraffin injections around 1900, liquid silicone from the early 1960s until concerns about its long-term effects led to its abandonment, bovine collagen from about 1980, and later products including hyaluronic acid gels (Restylane, Juvederm), calcium hydroxylapatite, PMMA microsphere products, autologous fat and donor dermal tissue [2]. Hyaluronic acid products are described as lasting roughly six months to a year or more, fat transfer as lasting longer but with potential lumping, and non-surgical options such as lip plumpers and suction devices as producing only temporary swelling [2].

A 2018 clinical review in which three facial plastic surgeons answered questions about injection, surgical enhancement, implants, complications and changing technique over the years gives an expert view of how implants fit alongside these options [9]. A 2022 scoping review of permanent lip enhancement notes that silicone implants and off-label permanent fillers are the two approaches used to obtain a permanent result, and that permanent fillers have no standard technique for correcting an unwanted outcome [10].

Wikipedia's lip-augmentation overview gives reported durations for the main alternatives: bovine collagen about four weeks to three months, Restylane about six months and sometimes longer, Juvederm up to a year to 18 months by manufacturer claims, calcium hydroxylapatite (Radiance) about two years on average in one 90-patient study, and fat transfer often lasting longer depending on movement and blood supply. PMMA microsphere fillers such as Artecoll/ArteFill remain permanently.[2] Implants differ from these in being a solid material that is neither absorbed nor injected into the lip tissue, so the volume and shape are set by the implant chosen at surgery.[2][7]

Temporary non-surgical options named in the same overview include lip plumpers, which irritate the lips to cause short-lived swelling, and suction pumps, which cause temporary swelling through vacuum pressure.[2] Fat grafting is described there as one of the best ways to maintain a semi-permanent, fuller, softer lip, and surgical flap augmentation as adding little volume and slight protrusion.[2]

A 2026 paper in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery notes that lip enhancement has traditionally been dominated by volumetric approaches, especially hyaluronic acid fillers, but that lip ageing also involves structural changes such as elongation of the cutaneous upper lip that fillers alone cannot address; the authors propose an anatomy-driven algorithm for choosing between techniques.[11] A 2018 expert review in which three facial plastic surgeons answered questions on injection, surgical enhancement, implants and complications describes the practitioner's side of this choice.[9]

A 1992 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described the gap that ePTFE was meant to fill: there was little literature on aesthetic lip enhancement, few reliable techniques using the patient's own tissue, and reluctance among surgeons to use an alloplastic implant in a mobile, superficial and exposed site. The authors reported PTFE grafts as a predictable, permanent option that could be customized, without visible scars or donor-site deformity [7].

By 2002 ePTFE had been used for lip and wrinkle augmentation for more than ten years, with excellent aesthetic results often reported alongside occasional complications, which prompted a redesigned implant [4]. Later, solid silicone prostheses were presented as a further development, and a 2017 retrospective series in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgery reported 100 patients along with technique tips [3].

Public interest in lip enhancement more broadly has been linked to celebrity publicity. A 2019 Google Trends analysis examined search volumes after Kylie Jenner's May 2015 announcement of lip augmentation and measured changes in public interest in lip procedures [12].
A 1992 report described permanent lip augmentation using PTFE grafts as a predictable option [7].

A 2002 study in Dermatologic Surgery treated 30 patients with 60 Advanta ePTFE implants for the lips, nasolabial folds or marionette lines. All patients had a natural-looking augmentation after 3-4 days of noticeable swelling, and the only significant complications were two upper lip implants removed for suspected infection. The authors concluded that the implants gave effective, natural-looking augmentation with minimal complications in a preliminary series [4].

A 2017 retrospective study in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgery treated 100 women with atrophic or hypoplastic lips using solid lip implants and presented the authors' technical tips [3].

In a 2020 study of 37 consecutive adults who had secondary cleft lip revision surgery, a single surgeon performed 15 lip revisions, 4 Abbe flaps, 12 dermal grafts and 6 PermaLip implants. Photographic measurements and examiner ratings found that in bilateral cleft patients Abbe flaps gave the largest improvement in upper lip projection, followed by PermaLip implants and dermal grafts, while in unilateral cleft patients PermaLip implants addressed impaired projection best [8].

Grokipedia cites a five-year study of 420 patients in which 25.4 percent moved from thin to normal lip classification [6]; this figure has not been independently verified. A 2023 StatPearls chapter gives a clinical overview [1], and a scoping review identified three retrospective studies, covering 73 patients and 111 lips, of surgical remodeling after permanent filler, a related category; it reported two early complications, one suture dehiscence and one total lip mucosa necrosis [10].

ePTFE complications reported in the literature include infection, extrusion, migration, shrinkage and hardening [4]. Wikipedia lists implant movement and extrusion, in which the implant breaks through the surface, among lip augmentation complications, together with swelling and bruising that can last from several days to a week [2]. Practitioners quoted by Wikipedia say that results depend heavily on the provider's skill and experience [2].

People with active cold sores, recurrent herpes simplex, bleeding disorders, active infection, lip scarring, or conditions such as diabetes or lupus that slow healing are listed by Wikipedia as groups who are generally advised against lip procedures, as are smokers because of slower healing [2].

Overfilling with any product can produce an exaggerated look sometimes called 'trout pout', and Wikipedia notes that overaggressive injection can cause lumps while too little can cause ridges.[2] In its summary of a calcium hydroxylapatite study, Wikipedia reports that 59 percent of patients had moderate to severe injection pain and four of 90 needed surgery for lip nodules; Artecoll has caused nodules and lumps, some requiring surgical removal.[2] Removal or revision of permanent material can be needed: a scoping review of surgical lip remodelling after permanent filler found the lack of a standard corrective technique to be the main issue.[10]

Liquid silicone used for lip augmentation, later abandoned over long-term concerns.[2]
Permanent lip augmentation with PTFE grafts reported.[7]
Newly designed ePTFE implant studied in 30 patients; the material had by then been used for lip augmentation for more than ten years.[4]
Kylie Jenner's May 2015 announcement of lip augmentation is followed by measurable changes in public search interest in lip procedures.[12]
Retrospective study of 100 women with solid lip implants.[3]
